Infectious mononucleosis: 3

A patient has a strongly suggestive early mononucleosis presentation but a negative heterophile test. Which testing principle explains why the result should not automatically end the evaluation when clinical suspicion remains substantial?

  1. Early negative heterophile testing does not exclude EBV
  2. Epstein-Barr virus infectious mononucleosis
  3. Reactive cytotoxic T lymphocytes
  4. An aminopenicillin-associated rash during EBV infection
  5. Splenic rupture risk
Answer and explanation

Early negative heterophile testing does not exclude EBV

Test sensitivity depends on timing and age; EBV-specific serology may be appropriate when suspicion persists.

Option explanations

Early negative heterophile testing does not exclude EBV: Test sensitivity depends on timing and age; EBV-specific serology may be appropriate when suspicion persists.

Epstein-Barr virus infectious mononucleosis: Fever, pharyngitis, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy and atypical lymphocytes are a classic presentation. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

Reactive cytotoxic T lymphocytes: The atypical lymphocytes in EBV mononucleosis are largely activated T cells responding to infected B cells. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

An aminopenicillin-associated rash during EBV infection: A rash after amoxicillin in EBV does not automatically establish permanent IgE-mediated penicillin allergy. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

Splenic rupture risk: Splenic enlargement during mononucleosis makes contact sports or abdominal trauma hazardous until medically cleared. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
